lessons.title: Food Commodities & Their Place in the Diet

before.content_html:
What Are Food Commodities?

Every ingredient you pull from the fridge or the store cupboard belongs to one of six major food commodity groups. Understanding what each group contributes to the diet, how to store it safely, and where it comes from is essential background knowledge for GCSE Food Preparation and Nutrition. The six groups are: fruit and vegetables; bread, cereals, flour, oats, rice, potatoes and pasta; milk, cheese and yoghurt; meat, fish, poultry and eggs; soya, tofu, beans, nuts and seeds; and butter, oils, margarine, sugar and syrup.

Key Fact

The six commodity groups must be learned as a list. Each group has a distinct nutritional role, set of characteristics, and storage requirement — all of which the written paper can test. Start here: fruit and vegetables / starchy foods / dairy / meat, fish and eggs / plant proteins / fats and sugars.

Fruit and Vegetables

Fruit and vegetables arrive fresh, frozen, dried, canned or juiced. Their main nutritional contribution is micronutrients — vitamin C (vital for immune function and iron absorption), vitamin A in the form of beta-carotene (found in orange and dark-green vegetables), folate (especially important in pregnancy), and potassium. They also supply dietary fibre, which aids digestion and reduces the risk of bowel disease. A plate of roasted root vegetables — carrots, sweet potato, parsnips — gives a useful hit of beta-carotene alongside natural sugars released by the dry heat.

Fresh fruit and vegetables should be stored in a cool, dark place or in the salad drawer of a refrigerator (≤5 °C) to slow enzymic browning and mould growth. Leafy greens wilt quickly once their cells lose moisture; keeping them cold and sealed slows this process. Canned and frozen forms are equally nutritious — freezing preserves micronutrients effectively because it halts enzyme activity almost completely. Origins vary by season: UK-grown tomatoes, runner beans and peas dominate the summer; imported tropical fruit (mangoes, pineapples) is available year-round but carries a higher food-miles cost.

Bread, Cereals, Flour, Oats, Rice, Potatoes and Pasta

Starchy foods are the body's main energy source, providing complex carbohydrates (polysaccharides) that release glucose gradually. Wholegrains — wholemeal bread, brown rice, oats — also supply B vitamins (particularly B1 thiamin), iron, and non-starch polysaccharides (dietary fibre). White refined versions have most of the bran removed, reducing fibre content but extending shelf life. A basic soda bread uses just flour, bicarbonate of soda, salt and buttermilk — illustrating how even a commodity as simple as flour behaves chemically (the acid in buttermilk reacts with the alkali bicarbonate to produce carbon dioxide, which lifts the dough).

Potatoes are tubers grown underground and should be stored in a cool, dark, dry location to prevent greening (solanine formation is triggered by light and is mildly toxic). Cereals and flours should be kept in sealed, dry containers away from moisture to prevent mould growth. Bread stales through starch retrogradation — wrapping it and keeping it at room temperature (not the refrigerator, which accelerates staling) extends freshness. UK wheat is grown primarily in East Anglia; rice is imported predominantly from Asia.

Milk, Cheese and Yoghurt

Dairy products supply high biological-value protein, calcium (critical for bone development in adolescents), phosphorus, vitamins A and D, and B vitamins including B12. A 200 ml glass of whole milk provides approximately 240 mg of calcium — about a quarter of the daily reference value for a teenager. Full-fat, semi-skimmed and skimmed variants differ in fat and fat-soluble vitamin content; skimmed milk has less fat-soluble vitamin A. Cheese making involves acid coagulation of casein proteins, while yoghurt is produced through the positive action of live Lactobacillus bacteria fermenting lactose into lactic acid.

Dairy must be stored below 5 °C in the refrigerator and used within the stated use-by date. Cross-contamination risk is high if raw meat drips onto dairy produce — always store raw meat on the bottom shelf. Long-life (UHT) milk is produced by heating to 135 °C for 2–4 seconds, destroying all bacteria; it can be stored at room temperature until opened. UK dairy farming is concentrated in the west of England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland, where rainfall supports grass growth for cattle.

Many students assume oat milk, almond milk or soya milk are nutritionally identical to cow’s milk. They are not — unless they are fortified. Cow’s milk naturally contains calcium (~120 mg per 100 ml), B12, and iodine. Most plant-based alternatives are low in these nutrients unless the manufacturer adds them. Soya milk is the closest match for protein quality (it provides all essential amino acids), but oat and almond milks are protein-poor. When planning a vegan diet or a dairy-free diet, always check the nutritional label and choose a fortified plant milk — especially for children and pregnant women whose calcium and B12 needs are high.

Meat, Fish, Poultry and Eggs

This group provides high biological-value protein (containing all nine essential amino acids), iron, zinc, B vitamins (particularly B12) and fat-soluble vitamins. Oily fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines — is an especially important source of omega-3 fatty acids (a polyunsaturated fat) and vitamin D. Eggs are nutritionally dense: one medium egg supplies 6 g of protein plus choline, selenium, and vitamins A and D. When a roast chicken goes into the oven, the proteins in the breast meat undergo denaturation as heat uncoils their molecular chains — making the flesh firm and opaque.

Raw meat, poultry and fish carry the highest contamination risk of any commodity group. They must be stored on the bottom shelf of the refrigerator (below 5 °C), wrapped to prevent drip, and used within the use-by date. Whole fish should ideally be cooked on the day of purchase or frozen immediately. Red meat is sourced primarily from UK cattle and sheep; white poultry from indoor and free-range farms; fish from UK coastal waters (cod, haddock, mackerel) and international fisheries.

Soya, Tofu, Beans, Nuts and Seeds

This group provides the main protein alternatives for vegetarians and vegans. Protein complementation is important here: most plant proteins are ‘incomplete’ (lacking one or more essential amino acids), but combining foods — for example, baked beans on wholegrain toast, or lentil dhal with rice — provides the full range. Soya and tofu are notable exceptions: they are ‘complete’ proteins. Beans and lentils also contribute iron, dietary fibre, B vitamins, and slow-release carbohydrate, making them an ideal base for a stew or curry. Nuts and seeds supply healthy unsaturated fats, vitamin E, magnesium, and zinc.

Dried pulses should be stored in airtight containers in a cool, dry cupboard. Tinned beans are convenient and nutritionally comparable to home-cooked dried beans (though they may contain added salt). Nuts can become rancid if exposed to heat and light — a cool, dark storage location extends shelf life significantly. Soya is primarily grown in South America (Brazil, Argentina) and the USA; UK production of pulses (field beans, peas) is increasing as a more sustainable domestic alternative.

Butter, Oils, Margarine, Sugar and Syrup

This group provides concentrated energy from fat (9 kcal per gram) and from sugar (4 kcal per gram). Butter is a saturated fat derived from cream; vegetable oils such as olive oil, rapeseed oil and sunflower oil are unsaturated and associated with better cardiovascular health. Margarine is produced by hydrogenation of liquid vegetable oils — early versions produced trans fats, which raised CVD risk; modern margarines use different methods to minimise trans fats. Sugar provides empty calories with no micronutrient value; current dietary guidelines recommend that free sugars make up no more than 5% of daily energy intake. In a Victoria sandwich, butter or margarine is creamed with sugar to trap air bubbles — a functional property called aeration.

Key Fact

Refrigerators should be set at or below 5 °C. Raw meat, fish and poultry must always be stored on the bottom shelf to prevent drip contamination of ready-to-eat foods stored below. Sugar and syrup are shelf-stable because their high sugar concentration reduces water activity, inhibiting microbial growth.

A use-by date is a food safety marker: the food must not be consumed after this date regardless of appearance or smell. It appears on high-risk perishables such as raw meat, fish, and ready-to-eat meals. A best-before date is a quality marker: food may still be safe to eat after this date but may be less fresh. It typically appears on shelf-stable products such as tinned food, pasta, and flour. Misreading these labels — particularly eating meat past its use-by date — is a significant cause of food poisoning.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the main nutritional function of the fruit and vegetables commodity group?
A) Providing saturated fats for energy storage
B) Providing high biological-value protein for tissue repair
C) Providing micronutrients such as vitamins and minerals
D) Providing polysaccharides as the body's primary fuel
practice_questions.marks: C) Providing micronutrients such as vitamins and minerals [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two commodity groups that are the main dietary sources of protein.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two from: meat, fish, poultry and eggs; soya, tofu, beans, nuts and seeds; milk, cheese and yoghurt. [1 mark for correctly naming two groups — no mark for only one group]

practice_questions.text: State two rules for storing raw meat safely in a domestic refrigerator.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct storage rule, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: store at or below 5 degrees C (1); keep on the bottom shelf to prevent drip contamination of other foods (1); keep covered or wrapped (1); use within the use-by date (1). Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how three different commodity groups contribute to a healthy, balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each well-described contribution, up to 3 marks. Each mark requires a named commodity group AND a described nutritional benefit. Example answers: starchy foods provide complex carbohydrates / polysaccharides which release energy gradually (1); fruit and vegetables supply vitamin C, minerals and dietary fibre to support the immune system and digestion (1); dairy products provide calcium and protein, which are important for bone development and tissue repair (1). Do not award marks for simply naming a group without describing its contribution.

practice_questions.text: Priya is 16 and follows a lacto-vegetarian diet. She eats dairy products but no meat, fish or eggs. Explain two ways Priya can ensure she gets enough protein from her diet.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per explanation (1 for the point, 1 for a linked reason using because/this means that/as a result), up to 4 marks. Acceptable points: she should combine plant protein foods such as baked beans with wholegrain toast, because most plant proteins are incomplete (lacking one or more essential amino acids) and combining two sources provides the full range (2); she can include dairy products such as milk, cheese and yoghurt, because dairy is a high biological-value protein that contains all nine essential amino acids (2); she can eat soya or tofu, because soya is a complete plant protein that provides all essential amino acids without the need for complementation (2). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why correct storage of food commodities is important for food safety and nutritional quality. In your answer, refer to at least two different commodity groups.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): Two or three well-developed explanations, each linked to a named commodity group. Answer uses food-science vocabulary (e.g. microbial growth, enzyme activity, cross-contamination, denaturation, water activity) and consistently applies because/this means that/as a result. Secure (3-4 marks): Relevant points for two commodity groups, mostly accurate, with some development of reasons. One or two links to cause and effect. Developing (1-2 marks): Points about storage stated without explanation; minimal use of commodity-group names; no cause-and-effect links. Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content. Indicative content: raw meat must be stored below 5 degrees C on the bottom shelf to prevent cross-contamination, because bacteria such as salmonella can transfer from raw meat drip to ready-to-eat foods stored below; fruit and vegetables should be stored in a cool, dark location because enzyme activity and mould growth are slowed at lower temperatures, preserving micronutrient content; starchy foods such as flour and pasta should be stored in airtight containers in a dry cupboard, because moisture triggers mould growth; sugar and syrup are shelf-stable because their high sugar concentration reduces water activity, making it difficult for micro-organisms to survive.

before.content_html:
Why Commodities Behave Differently in the Kitchen

Pick up a raw egg and a hard-boiled one — they feel and behave completely differently, yet the only thing that changed was heat. This is the heart of food science: every commodity has working characteristics that determine what happens when you cook with it. Understanding these characteristics explains why a sponge cake rises, why a sauce thickens, why a stir-fry browns — and crucially, why things can go wrong.

Key Fact

The spec lists ten functional / chemical properties across four ingredient categories. Learn them in groups: carbohydrates (gelatinisation, dextrinization); fats (shortening, aeration, plasticity, emulsification); proteins (coagulation, foam formation, gluten formation, denaturation); fruit and vegetables (enzymic browning, oxidisation).

Carbohydrates: Gelatinisation and Dextrinization

Gelatinisation is what turns a thin liquid into a thick sauce. When a roux-based béchamel sauce is heated on the hob, the starch granules in the flour absorb water, swell and eventually burst, releasing amylose chains that tangle together and thicken the sauce. The process is essentially complete above 80 °C. If the sauce is not stirred during this stage, clumps of gelatinised starch form — the lumpy white sauce so familiar from school kitchens. Stirring distributes the heat evenly and keeps the granules from aggregating.

Dextrinization happens when starch is dry-heated. Toast the surface of a slice of bread under the grill and you will see dextrinization at work: the starch molecules on the surface break down into shorter chains (dextrins), producing the golden-brown colour and slightly crisp texture of toast. This is a different reaction from gelatinisation, which requires water. Dextrinization also contributes to the crust of a baked loaf and the croutons in a salad.

Fats: Shortening, Aeration, Plasticity and Emulsification

Fats are among the most functionally versatile commodities. Shortening describes the way fat coats flour particles and prevents gluten strands from forming long networks — this is exactly what you want in shortcrust pastry, where the goal is a crumbly, tender texture rather than chew. Aeration occurs when fat (butter or margarine) is creamed vigorously with sugar: the mechanical action forces air into the fat, creating tiny bubbles that expand in the oven and contribute to a light sponge. Plasticity refers to the ability of solid fats to be spread, rolled or moulded at room temperature — important for laminated pastries such as croissants, where butter must be rolled into layers without melting. Emulsification is the ability to hold oil and water together. Egg yolk contains lecithin, a natural emulsifier, which is why adding egg yolk to a vinaigrette produces a temporarily stable suspension, and why hollandaise sauce can hold butter in a water-based liquid without separating.

Proteins: Coagulation, Foam Formation, Gluten Formation and Denaturation

Coagulation is the reason scrambled eggs solidify when heated: liquid egg protein denatures and then bonds together, forming a solid curd. In a quiche filling, the protein in the egg-and-milk mixture sets in the oven, encasing the other ingredients. A related property is foam formation: whisking egg whites stretches and denatures the protein, which wraps around tiny air bubbles and stabilises them — giving a meringue mixture its volume. The foam collapses if fat is accidentally introduced (a trace of egg yolk, a greasy bowl), because fat destroys the protein film around the air bubbles.

Gluten formation occurs in wheat-flour doughs. Glutenin and gliadin proteins in flour absorb water and, when the dough is kneaded, align and bond into a continuous elastic network. This network traps carbon dioxide produced by yeast fermentation, causing the dough to rise. Over-working a pastry dough activates the same protein network, producing a tough, chewy result instead of a short, crumbly one — which is why pastry-making guides say “handle the dough as little as possible.”

Students often use these terms interchangeably — but they describe different stages. Denaturation is the unfolding of the protein molecule’s three-dimensional shape. It can be caused by heat (frying an egg), acid (marinating chicken in lemon juice tightens the flesh), or physical action (whisking egg whites). Coagulation is the next stage: the denatured (unfolded) proteins bond together, forming a solid structure. Both processes are irreversible. In an exam question about why scrambled egg solidifies, the full answer is: “The proteins in the egg denature as they are heated (because heat breaks the bonds holding the protein in its three-dimensional shape); the denatured proteins then coagulate, bonding together to form a solid curd.”

Fruit and Vegetables: Enzymic Browning and Oxidisation

Enzymic browning is why a freshly sliced apple turns brown within minutes of being cut. The cut surface exposes phenolic compounds to polyphenol oxidase enzymes; these react with oxygen from the air to produce brown melanin pigments. In cooking, enzymic browning can be prevented by: covering the cut surface with acidulated water (vitamin C from lemon juice lowers pH, inhibiting the enzyme); blanching (brief boiling denatures the enzyme); or vacuum packing (removing oxygen). In the production of black tea, enzymic browning is deliberately encouraged to develop colour and flavour. Oxidisation is the broader term for nutrient loss (particularly vitamin C) when fruit and vegetables are cut, stored or cooked — oxygen in the air, heat and water all accelerate the process.

Dry vs Moist Methods of Cooking

The cooking method determines which of a commodity’s working characteristics are activated. Dry methods include roasting, baking, grilling, frying and dry-frying. In dry methods, surface moisture evaporates quickly, temperatures at the surface can reach well above 100 °C, and reactions like dextrinization, the Maillard reaction, and fat rendering take place. A Sunday roast chicken in the oven is a showcase for dry-heat cooking: the proteins denature and coagulate in the breast, fat renders from the skin, and the Maillard reaction creates the brown crust and rich flavour. Moist methods include boiling, steaming, poaching, braising and stewing. Water limits temperatures to 100 °C at atmospheric pressure; this prevents surface browning but can cause water-soluble vitamins (B vitamins, vitamin C) to leach into the cooking water. Steaming is preferable to boiling for retaining micronutrients in vegetables.

Key Fact

The Maillard reaction requires amino acids AND reducing sugars AND a temperature above approximately 140 °C. It produces brown colour and complex flavour. It is responsible for the crust of a loaf of bread, the colour of a grilled steak, and the golden skin of a roast potato. It is NOT the same as caramelisation, which involves only sugar.

A very common exam error is to confuse these two starch reactions. Remember: gelatinisation needs water (it thickens a sauce, a gravy, or a custard); dextrinization needs dry heat (it browns the surface of toast, bread crusts, and croutons). Both involve starch molecules changing structure, but they are triggered by completely different conditions. A quick mnemonic: “G for gravy (gelatinisation), D for dry-toasted (dextrinization).”
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The ten key working characteristics to know are: gelatinisation and dextrinization (carbohydrates); shortening, aeration, plasticity and emulsification (fats); coagulation, foam formation, gluten formation and denaturation (proteins); enzymic browning and oxidisation (fruit and vegetables).
  • Dry methods (roasting, baking, grilling) activate browning reactions (Maillard, dextrinization) because temperatures can exceed 100 °C; moist methods (boiling, steaming) limit temperature to 100 °C and can cause water-soluble vitamin loss.
  • Denaturation (unfolding of protein) and coagulation (bonding of unfolded proteins) are two distinct, sequential stages — using both terms correctly in an exam answer shows precise knowledge.

before.content_html:
Defining Micronutrients

The spec gives a precise definition here too: micronutrients are “required by humans throughout life in small quantities to facilitate a range of physiological functions.” Unlike macronutrients (protein, fats, carbohydrates), which are consumed in gram amounts, micronutrients are needed in milligram or even microgram quantities. The two categories are vitamins and minerals (plus trace elements). Despite their small quantities, deficiency — or excess — of any micronutrient has measurable health consequences.

Key Fact

Fat-soluble vitamins on the spec: A and D. Water-soluble vitamins: B1 (thiamin), B2 (riboflavin), B3 (niacin), B9 (folic acid / folate), B12 (cobalamin) and vitamin C. Fat-soluble vitamins dissolve in fat and can be stored in the liver; water-soluble vitamins cannot be stored and are lost in cooking water — a key reason steaming is preferable to boiling vegetables.

Fat-Soluble Vitamins: A and D

Vitamin A exists in two forms: retinol (from animal sources such as liver, oily fish, eggs and dairy) and beta-carotene (a provitamin found in orange and dark-green vegetables such as carrots, sweet potato, spinach — converted to vitamin A in the body). Its functions include: maintaining normal vision in dim light (deficiency causes night blindness); supporting the immune system; and maintaining healthy skin and mucous membranes. Excess vitamin A from supplements is toxic and teratogenic in pregnancy — pregnant women are advised not to eat liver for this reason. Fat is needed in the diet for vitamin A to be absorbed, because it is fat-soluble.

Vitamin D is uniquely made in the skin through exposure to UVB sunlight — during UK winters (October to March), sunlight is too weak to trigger synthesis, so dietary sources become critical. Food sources include oily fish (salmon, sardines), egg yolk, and fortified foods (some cereals, margarine, plant milks). Its primary function is to promote calcium absorption in the gut, enabling bone mineralisation and muscle function. Deficiency causes rickets in children (soft, bowed bones) and osteomalacia (soft, painful bones) in adults. The NHS recommends a 10 μg vitamin D supplement for everyone in the UK during autumn and winter.

Water-Soluble Vitamins: B Group and Vitamin C

The B vitamins work primarily as coenzymes — they help enzymes release energy from macronutrients. They are water-soluble, so they cannot be stored in the body, and must be consumed regularly. Key B vitamins on the spec:

B1 (thiamin) — supports the release of energy from carbohydrates; found in wholegrain cereals, pork, peas. Deficiency: beriberi (nerve and heart damage), seen historically in populations reliant on polished white rice. B2 (riboflavin) — assists energy release from all macronutrients; found in dairy, meat, eggs and green vegetables. Deficiency: sore throat, cracked lips, and inflamed tongue. B3 (niacin) — needed for energy release and DNA repair; found in meat, fish, wheat flour, eggs. Severe deficiency: pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia). B9 (folic acid / folate) — essential for DNA synthesis and cell division; found in leafy green vegetables, fortified cereals, pulses, liver. Critical in the first twelve weeks of pregnancy: deficiency causes neural tube defects (spina bifida) in the developing foetus. Women planning a pregnancy are advised to take a 400 μg supplement daily. B12 (cobalamin) — required for red blood cell formation and nerve function; found exclusively in animal products (meat, fish, eggs, dairy). Vegans are at high risk of B12 deficiency and must supplement or eat fortified foods (fortified plant milks, nutritional yeast). Deficiency causes pernicious anaemia and neurological damage.

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is vital for: collagen synthesis (the protein that forms connective tissue, skin and blood vessel walls); immune function; and the absorption of non-haem iron from plant foods (vitamin C reduces ferric iron to the more absorbable ferrous form). A glass of orange juice with a bowl of iron-fortified cereal significantly improves iron uptake — an example of complementary nutrient action. Deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums, poor wound healing, bruising). Vitamin C is heat-labile and water-soluble, making it the most vulnerable vitamin during cooking — another reason to prefer steaming over boiling.

Vitamin B12 is found only in animal products — no plant food contains it naturally. A fully vegan diet (no meat, fish, dairy or eggs) will lead to B12 deficiency unless the person supplements or eats fortified foods such as nutritional yeast, fortified plant milks or fortified cereals. Deficiency develops slowly because the liver can store B12 for years, but once depleted, the consequences (pernicious anaemia, nerve damage) are serious. Vitamin D is also a concern for vegans because the best food sources are oily fish and egg yolk. In the UK, where sunlight is insufficient for half the year, a 10 μg daily supplement is recommended for everyone — and especially for vegans who cannot rely on dietary animal-food sources.

Minerals: Calcium, Iron, Potassium and Magnesium

Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body — 99% is in bones and teeth. It requires vitamin D for absorption. Adolescents have particularly high calcium needs during the rapid bone growth of puberty. Deficiency over a lifetime leads to osteoporosis (reduced bone density) and increased fracture risk. Sources: dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens, tinned fish with bones (sardines, salmon). Iron comes in two forms: haem iron (in red meat and offal — highly absorbable) and non-haem iron (in fortified cereals, dark-green vegetables, pulses — less absorbable, but absorption is improved by vitamin C). Deficiency causes iron-deficiency anaemia: reduced haemoglobin production means less oxygen is carried in the blood, resulting in fatigue, pallor and breathlessness. Teenage girls and women of childbearing age are at highest risk due to iron losses during menstruation.

Potassium maintains fluid balance, supports nerve impulse transmission and helps regulate blood pressure. Found in bananas, potatoes, spinach, pulses and dairy. Adequate potassium intake is associated with reduced risk of hypertension (high blood pressure). Magnesium is needed for enzyme activity, muscle contraction and bone health. Found in nuts, seeds, wholegrains, dark-green vegetables. Deficiency symptoms include muscle cramps, fatigue and irregular heartbeat.

Trace Elements: Iodine and Fluoride

Iodine is required to synthesise thyroid hormones (thyroxine), which regulate metabolic rate, body temperature, and growth. Sources: seafood, dairy, eggs. Deficiency causes goitre (enlarged thyroid gland) and, in children, cretinism (impaired brain development and stunted growth). Many people in the UK obtain iodine through dairy, but vegans who avoid dairy and seafood are at risk — some plant milks are now fortified with iodine. Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel by incorporating into the crystalline structure of the mineral hydroxyapatite, making teeth more resistant to acid attack from bacteria. It is found naturally in some water supplies (water fluoridation is practised in some UK regions), in tea, and in fluoride toothpaste. Deficiency: increased susceptibility to dental caries (tooth decay). Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis (white or brown mottling of teeth).

Key Fact

Six deficiency conditions to know: vitamin D → rickets (children) / osteomalacia (adults); vitamin C → scurvy; iron → iron-deficiency anaemia; calcium (lifetime deficiency) → osteoporosis; folate (in pregnancy) → neural tube defects (spina bifida); B12 → pernicious anaemia and nerve damage. These cause-and-effect pairs are high-frequency exam content.

Dietary Value of Water

Water is not a nutrient in the macronutrient / micronutrient sense, but it is essential for life. The body is approximately 60% water by weight. Water’s functions include: transporting nutrients and oxygen in the blood; removing waste products (urea via the kidneys); regulating body temperature through sweating and breathing; providing a medium for all chemical reactions in cells; and lubricating joints. Adults in the UK are advised to drink approximately 6–8 glasses (1.5–2 litres) of fluid per day — more in hot weather or during exercise. Dehydration reduces concentration, causes headaches, and — if severe — impairs kidney function. For a teenager playing football for 90 minutes in summer, fluid replacement during and after the match is critical to maintain performance and avoid heat exhaustion.

Dietary Fibre (NSP)

Dietary fibre (non-starch polysaccharides, NSP) is the indigestible part of plant cell walls — found in wholegrain cereals, fruit, vegetables, pulses, nuts and seeds. Because it cannot be digested in the small intestine, it passes to the colon, where it: bulks out faeces and speeds intestinal transit (reducing the risk of constipation and bowel cancer); feeds beneficial bacteria (promoting a healthy gut microbiome); and slows glucose absorption after a meal (helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels). Adequate fibre intake also promotes satiety — the feeling of fullness — which can help manage weight. The UK recommendation is 30 g of fibre per day for adults; most people consume closer to 18 g. Switching from white bread to wholemeal, or adding a portion of pulses to a stew, makes a significant difference.

Some nutrients depend on other nutrients to work properly. Three important complementary pairs: (1) Vitamin C and iron — vitamin C in the small intestine converts ferric iron (from plant sources) to ferrous iron, which is absorbed more efficiently. Adding lemon juice to a lentil dish or drinking orange juice with cereal are practical examples. (2) Vitamin D and calcium — vitamin D promotes the production of calcium-binding proteins in the gut wall, enabling calcium to be absorbed into the bloodstream. Without adequate vitamin D, dietary calcium largely passes through unabsorbed. (3) B vitamins working together — several B vitamins act as coenzymes in the same metabolic pathways; a deficiency in one can impair the action of another. Understanding these complementary actions is required by the spec and often tested in extended response questions about planning diets for specific individuals.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Micronutrients are required in small quantities to support physiological functions. Fat-soluble vitamins (A and D) are stored in the liver; water-soluble vitamins (B group and C) are not stored and are lost in cooking water — making cooking method important for nutritional preservation.
  • Six key deficiency conditions: rickets/osteomalacia (vitamin D); scurvy (vitamin C); iron-deficiency anaemia (iron); osteoporosis (calcium, long-term); neural tube defects (folate, in pregnancy); pernicious anaemia (B12, especially vegans). These cause-and-effect pairs are high-frequency exam content.
  • Water and dietary fibre (NSP) are not vitamins or minerals, but both are essential. Water underpins every chemical reaction in the body; NSP (30 g/day recommended) supports bowel health, stable blood sugar and satiety.

before.content_html:
What Is the Recommended Daily Intake?

Every nutrient has a recommended daily intake (RDI) — a target figure that represents what a healthy person needs over a day. For energy, the broad adult benchmarks are roughly 2,000 kcal for women and 2,500 kcal for men, but these change dramatically depending on age, body size and activity level. The RDI is not a precise prescription; it is a planning tool that helps you check whether a recipe, a school dinner menu or a family’s weekly shop is broadly on track.

When looking at percentage energy values, the current guidelines recommend roughly 50% of daily energy from carbohydrates (of which free sugars no more than 5%), 35% from fats (saturated fat below 11%) and around 15% from protein. Dietary fibre (non-soluble polysaccharides, or NSP) is targeted at 30 g per day for adults, though many people fall well short of this. Vitamins and minerals do not contribute energy but each has its own RDI — for example, 700 mg calcium per day for adults, rising sharply during teenage growth spurts.

Key Fact

Current healthy-eating guidelines suggest approximately 50% of energy from carbohydrates, 35% from fats and 15% from protein. Free sugars should account for no more than 5% of total energy intake.

Basal Metabolic Rate and Physical Activity Level

Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the energy a body burns just to stay alive — heart beating, lungs breathing, cells repairing. It is influenced by body size (a bigger body burns more), age (BMR falls as lean muscle mass declines after about 30), sex (males typically have higher BMR due to greater muscle mass) and hormones. BMR alone, however, does not tell you how much food someone needs in a day; you also need to account for how active they are.

Physical activity level (PAL) multiplies BMR to give total daily energy need. A sedentary office worker has a PAL of about 1.4; a moderately active person (some exercise three times a week) scores around 1.6–1.7; a highly active person such as a construction worker or competitive athlete may reach 1.9 or above. So a teenage boy with a BMR of 1,800 kcal and a PAL of 1.7 needs roughly 3,060 kcal per day — considerably more than the adult average.

Many students write “BMR is the energy someone needs each day” and leave it there. That misses the point. BMR is only the resting baseline — the energy a comatose person would use. To find out how much food a real person actually needs, you multiply their BMR by their PAL. A nurse working a 12-hour shift needs far more than their BMR; a convalescing elderly patient recovering in bed needs very little above it. Exam questions will often give you a BMR value and a PAL and ask you to calculate or explain the total energy requirement.

Energy Balance and Healthy Body Weight

Energy balance is the relationship between calories in and calories out. When the two are equal, body weight stays stable. A consistent positive energy balance (eating more than you burn) leads to weight gain as excess energy is stored as adipose tissue. A consistent negative energy balance leads to weight loss as the body draws on stored fat and, eventually, muscle protein. Understanding energy balance is central to planning diets for weight management, sports performance and recovery from illness.

How Nutritional Needs Change Across Life Stages

Nutritional needs are not fixed from birth to old age — they shift at every major life stage in response to growth, hormonal change, activity levels and the risk of age-related conditions. The six broad life stages examined are: toddlers (1–3), primary-aged children (4–10), teenagers (11–18), early adulthood (19–50), middle adulthood (51–64) and late adulthood (65+).

Toddlers (1–3 Years)

Toddlers are growing rapidly and need energy-dense food relative to their small stomach size. Full-fat dairy is recommended — they must NOT be given semi-skimmed or skimmed milk as their main drink before age two because they need the fat-soluble vitamins A and D that whole milk provides. Iron is a key nutrient because breast milk iron stores from birth deplete around six months; by toddler age, red meat, fortified cereals and leafy greens are important sources. Vitamin D is widely deficient in the UK population; toddlers are advised to take a daily supplement.

Teenagers (11–18 Years)

Teenagers undergo rapid skeletal and muscular growth driven by sex hormones. Calcium and vitamin D are critical — up to 45% of peak bone mass is laid down during adolescence. The RDI for calcium rises to around 1,000 mg per day for 11–18-year-olds (higher than the adult requirement of 700 mg). Girls who have started menstruation have significantly elevated iron needs — around 14.8 mg per day — because menstrual blood loss depletes iron stores. Teenage boys have higher protein and energy needs than girls, especially if involved in sport. Despite these elevated needs, many teenagers skip breakfast, eat too many free sugars and consume below-target NSP — a pattern that exam questions often ask students to explain and correct.

Key Fact

Teenagers need approximately 1,000 mg of calcium per day — more than adults — because up to 45% of peak bone mass is built during adolescence. Girls who have started their period need around 14.8 mg of iron daily to replace losses from menstruation.

Early and Middle Adulthood (19–64 Years)

Energy needs peak in the twenties and thirties, particularly for physically active adults. After age 30, BMR begins a gradual decline as lean muscle mass reduces, so calorie needs fall even if activity stays constant. Pregnancy and breastfeeding increase specific nutrient requirements: folic acid (400 mcg/day in early pregnancy to reduce neural tube defect risk), iron, calcium and omega-3 fatty acids. Middle adulthood brings rising risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD), type 2 diabetes and obesity, making it especially important to monitor saturated fat, free sugars and salt intake.

Late Adulthood (65+ Years)

Energy needs fall in late adulthood as activity typically decreases, yet protein needs remain high — or may even increase slightly — to help maintain muscle mass and support immune function. Vitamin D supplementation is recommended for all adults over 65 because reduced skin synthesis (less time outdoors, thinner skin) limits natural production. Calcium remains important to slow the rate of bone density loss. Constipation is common, so maintaining adequate NSP and fluid intake is key. Appetite often decreases, so older adults risk under-eating despite needing nutrient-dense meals.

Consider Arthur, 70, who lives alone and rarely goes outside during winter. He has a small appetite, a limited pension budget and his GP has flagged low vitamin D. A well-planned meal for Arthur would be nutrient-dense but portion-small: a serving of oily fish (vitamin D, omega-3), steamed broccoli and carrots (NSP, vitamin C, folate), a jacket potato (potassium, NSP) and a glass of full-fat milk (calcium, vitamins A and D). The cooking method matters — steaming the vegetables preserves vitamin C losses better than boiling. A dessert of fortified yoghurt adds further calcium and vitamin D without a large calorie load.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Total daily energy requirement is calculated by multiplying BMR (the body’s resting energy use) by PAL (a multiplier for physical activity). Energy balance — calories in versus calories out — determines whether body weight stays stable, rises or falls.
  • Percentage energy guidelines suggest roughly 50% carbohydrates, 35% fats and 15% protein, with free sugars capped at 5% of energy and NSP targeted at 30 g per day for adults.
  • Nutritional needs change at every life stage: toddlers need full-fat dairy and iron; teenagers need high calcium (1,000 mg/day) and iron (especially girls); older adults need vitamin D supplements, adequate protein and NSP despite falling energy needs.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes basal metabolic rate (BMR)?
A) The total energy a person uses including exercise
B) The minimum energy the body needs at rest to maintain vital functions
C) The number of calories in a food per 100 g
D) The recommended daily intake of protein for adults
practice_questions.marks: B) The minimum energy the body needs at rest to maintain vital functions [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the two factors multiplied together to calculate a person's total daily energy requirement.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for both correct: basal metabolic rate (BMR) and physical activity level (PAL). Both must be named for the mark.

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why teenagers have higher calcium needs than adults.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each correct reason, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers include: rapid skeletal growth during puberty; up to 45% of peak bone mass is formed during adolescence; the calcium RDI for teenagers (approximately 1,000 mg) exceeds the adult RDI (700 mg); bone density is at its most responsive to calcium intake during teenage years.

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways in which the nutritional needs of a toddler aged two differ from those of an adult woman.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each distinct, described difference, up to 3 marks. Acceptable answers include: toddlers need full-fat dairy for fat-soluble vitamins A and D (semi-skimmed not recommended under age 2); toddlers have proportionally high energy needs relative to their small body size; toddlers need iron-rich foods (e.g. red meat, fortified cereals) because birth iron stores from breast milk are depleted by 6 months; toddlers may need a daily vitamin D supplement as UK dietary sources are limited; adult women in pregnancy or breastfeeding have elevated folic acid needs not shared by toddlers.

practice_questions.text: Priya is a 16-year-old who plays football for her school team three times a week. Her mum is concerned that Priya often skips breakfast and relies on sugary snacks. Explain why Priya's energy and nutrient requirements are higher than those of a sedentary adult woman of the same weight.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for each linked cause-and-effect point, up to 4. Acceptable chains include: Priya is still growing (a teenager), so her BMR is higher than an adult's because her body is using energy for tissue building as well as maintenance (1+1); her high PAL (regular sport) multiplies her BMR to a considerably higher total energy requirement than a sedentary adult (1+1); she is in peak bone-building adolescence so her calcium RDI is higher (1) because 45% of peak bone mass forms during teenage years (1); girls who menstruate have higher iron needs (1) because monthly blood loss depletes iron stores (1). Award a maximum of 4 marks with the 'because/this means that/as a result' links present.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how energy requirements change across two different life stages, and analyse the key factors that explain these differences.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Clear discussion of at least two life stages with specific RDI or nutrient figures cited; BMR and PAL both used as analytical tools; at least two factors (e.g. growth rate, hormonal changes, activity level, pregnancy, age-related muscle loss) analysed with cause-and-effect reasoning; applies to named or plausible real eaters (e.g. a teenage athlete, a pregnant woman, an elderly person); accurate food-science vocabulary throughout; both sides of each contrast clearly developed.

Secure (5-6 marks): Two life stages discussed with mostly accurate content; at least one specific RDI or PAL value cited; some cause-and-effect reasoning; one or two analytical points developed but not all sustained; generally accurate vocabulary.

Developing (3-4 marks): Two life stages mentioned but mostly described rather than analysed; limited use of BMR/PAL framework; facts stated without 'because' chains; may be one-sided (only one life stage developed).

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic and/or partially correct points about one or two life stages; little or no analytical framework; no specific RDI or nutrient values; listing rather than discussion.

right: Full-fat dairy for vitamins A and D; iron-rich foods

before.content_html:
Why Calculate Nutritional Values?

A recipe is more than a list of ingredients — it is a nutritional delivery system. Calculating the energy and nutrient content of a recipe, a meal or a day’s eating tells you whether the food you are planning actually meets the needs of the person eating it. This skill underpins practical decision-making: a school cook planning a canteen menu for a mixed-age cohort, a community dietitian advising a patient with type 2 diabetes, and a food technologist reformulating a product to reduce saturated fat all rely on the same fundamental process. In your exam, you may be given a recipe with per-100g nutritional data and asked to calculate values for a specific serving size, identify a deficiency or excess, and propose targeted changes.

The Calculation Method: Step by Step

Nutritional values for individual ingredients are almost always provided per 100 g. To find the value for the quantity used in a recipe, the calculation is:

Nutrient value = (amount of ingredient used in grams ÷ 100) × nutrient per 100 g

You then sum these values across all ingredients to get the total for the whole recipe. To find the value per portion, divide the total by the number of portions the recipe makes. This same process applies whether you are calculating energy (in kcal or kJ), grams of fat, grams of saturated fat, grams of carbohydrate, grams of free sugars, grams of protein, or milligrams of a micronutrient such as calcium or iron.

A basic shortcrust pastry uses 200 g plain flour (fat: 1.4 g per 100 g) and 100 g butter (fat: 82 g per 100 g). Calculate the total fat in the pastry before baking:

Flour fat: (200 ÷ 100) × 1.4 = 2.0 × 1.4 = 2.8 g

Butter fat: (100 ÷ 100) × 82 = 1.0 × 82 = 82 g

Total fat in whole pastry: 2.8 + 82 = 84.8 g

If the recipe makes 8 portions: 84.8 ÷ 8 = 10.6 g fat per portion.

This immediately tells us the pastry is butter-dominated and that replacing even half the butter with a lower-fat alternative would have a large impact. Show every step in your exam answer — the working earns marks even if you make an arithmetic error at the final step.

Calculating Energy

Energy in food comes from three macronutrients: protein, fat and carbohydrate. The energy values used in calculations are: protein: 4 kcal per gram; carbohydrate: 3.75 kcal per gram; fat: 9 kcal per gram. Alcohol yields 7 kcal per gram but is not normally the focus of GCSE calculations. Notice that fat is more than twice as energy-dense as protein or carbohydrate — this explains why even a small quantity of butter, oil or cream raises the calorie count of a recipe considerably. When a recipe declares “350 kcal per serving”, you can work backwards to check plausibility: if the serving contains 12 g fat (12 × 9 = 108 kcal from fat), 30 g carbohydrate (30 × 3.75 = 112.5 kcal) and 14 g protein (14 × 4 = 56 kcal), the total is approximately 276 kcal — so you would know the label figure seems slightly high and there may be other contributors (e.g. alcohol).

Key Fact

Energy yield: protein = 4 kcal/g, carbohydrate = 3.75 kcal/g, fat = 9 kcal/g. Fat is more than twice as energy-dense as protein or carbohydrate, which is why small quantities of butter or oil significantly increase a recipe’s calorie total.

Using Nutritional Data to Make Targeted Changes

Calculating nutritional values is only useful if it drives a decision. Once you have the numbers, you can compare them against the relevant RDI and identify which nutrients are over or under the target. The spec identifies three common scenarios:

Increasing dietary fibre (NSP): If a recipe or day’s eating is low in NSP, evidence-based changes include switching white flour to wholemeal (the bran layer is retained), adding pulses (lentils, chickpeas) to a stew or soup, including oats in a crumble topping, choosing wholegrain bread and pasta, or adding vegetables such as broccoli or carrots to a sauce. Each of these changes adds measurable NSP grams while keeping the dish recognisable.

Reducing saturated fat: A high saturated fat intake raises LDL cholesterol and increases CVD risk. Recipe changes that reduce saturated fat include: replacing butter with a reduced-fat spread or using olive oil (which is mainly monounsaturated); replacing full-fat cream in a sauce with low-fat natural yoghurt or a cornflour-thickened stock; trimming visible fat from meat before cooking; swapping a cream-based dessert for a fruit-based one. The impact can be quantified: replacing 50 g butter (82 g fat per 100 g, of which about 52% is saturated) with 50 g olive oil (100% fat, of which about 15% is saturated) significantly lowers the saturated fat even though the total fat barely changes.

Meeting free sugar recommendations: Current guidance recommends free sugars should not exceed 5% of total energy intake (about 30 g for an average adult). A recipe audit often reveals that free sugars come from unexpected sources: ketchup, low-fat yoghurt, ready-made pasta sauces, flavoured drinks and breakfast cereals. Swapping honey or sugar for mashed banana in a bake, replacing a sugary yoghurt with plain natural yoghurt, and removing juice from a meal and replacing it with water are all evidence-based, calculable changes.

Key Fact

Three targeted dietary changes: switch to wholemeal flour (adds NSP); replace butter with olive oil (reduces saturated fat while keeping fat type unsaturated); swap a sugary sauce for a tomato-based one with no added sugar (reduces free sugars). Each change can be quantified using per-100 g data.

A “low-fat” label means the product has been reformulated to reduce fat content compared to the standard version. However, manufacturers often compensate by adding more free sugars or starch to maintain the texture and palatability that fat previously provided. A low-fat fruit yoghurt might have 0.1 g fat per 100 g but 15 g sugar per 100 g — higher in energy than a full-fat plain yoghurt with 3.5 g fat and 5 g natural lactose. The lesson: always calculate both fat and total energy (kcal) and check the sugar line on the label, not just the fat line.

Energy Balance and Healthy Body Weight

Nutritional calculations become particularly powerful when applied to energy balance planning. If you know a person’s total daily energy requirement (BMR × PAL) and you calculate the energy content of their current diet, you can identify whether they are in a positive (weight-gaining), negative (weight-losing) or neutral (weight-stable) balance. This informs targeted changes: for a person who needs to lose weight gradually, a 200–500 kcal daily deficit achieved by reducing portion sizes and swapping high-energy-density foods for lower-density alternatives is safer and more sustainable than drastic restriction.

lessons.title: Heat Transfer & Why We Cook Food

before.content_html:
Why Do We Cook Food at All?

Raw ingredients are not always safe, digestible, palatable or appealing. Cooking transforms them along five dimensions: digestion (softening cellulose and denaturing proteins makes them easier to break down in the gut), taste (the Maillard reaction between amino acids and sugars, and caramelisation, produce hundreds of flavour compounds that raw food lacks), texture (collagen converts to gelatine, starches swell and thicken, proteins coagulate and firm up), appearance (browning, colour change, setting), and safety (heat kills the majority of pathogenic bacteria and denatures harmful enzymes). A raw chicken leg contains the same protein content as a roasted one, but it is unsafe to eat, tough and unappealing; cooking achieves all five goals simultaneously.

The Three Methods of Heat Transfer

Heat always moves from a hotter area to a cooler one. There are three distinct mechanisms by which this happens in a kitchen, and they work differently. Understanding which method (or combination) is at work in a given cooking process is high-tariff exam content.

Conduction is heat transfer by direct contact. Molecules in a hot frying pan vibrate rapidly and transfer that vibration energy to neighbouring molecules in the food touching the pan. Heat travels through the food from the outside layer inward, molecule by molecule. Conduction is slowest through poor thermal conductors (like the air pockets inside a bread loaf) and fastest through metals. A searing steak in a cast-iron pan relies on conduction to form its crust — the hot metal surface transfers heat directly to the meat protein, triggering the Maillard browning reaction within seconds of contact.

Convection happens in liquids and gases. When water or air near a heat source warms up, it becomes less dense and rises; cooler liquid or air sinks to take its place, creating circulating currents. These currents carry heat to the food from all sides. Boiling a potato in water uses convection: the hot water circulates around the potato, delivering heat evenly. A conventional oven with a fan (fan oven) uses forced convection — the fan speeds up the hot air circulation, reducing cooking time and improving evenness. A conventional oven without a fan relies on natural convection, which is slower and less even (the top of the oven is typically hotter than the bottom because hot air rises).

Radiation transfers heat as infrared electromagnetic waves that travel through space without needing a medium. The food does not need to touch the heat source or be surrounded by a hot fluid — the waves simply reach the food surface and are absorbed. Grilling under a gas or electric grill is the classic example: the glowing heating element or gas flame emits infrared radiation that browns and cooks the surface of the sausage, fish fillet or bread slice beneath it. Toasting bread relies almost entirely on radiation from the toaster elements.

Key Fact

Three methods of heat transfer: conduction (direct contact — frying steak in a pan), convection (circulating currents — boiling a potato, baking in a fan oven), radiation (infrared waves — grilling a sausage, toasting bread).

Key Fact

The Maillard reaction begins at approximately 140°C — which is why boiling cannot brown food (water limits temperature to 100°C) while frying, roasting and grilling can. Cast iron is one of the best conductors of heat in a kitchen: it reaches and holds high temperatures evenly, making it ideal for searing meat where Maillard browning is desired.

Many students identify one method of heat transfer and stop. The spec is explicit that students must understand how “the production of some dishes relies on more than one method of heat transference.” Consider baking a jacket potato in a conventional oven: conduction transfers heat from the hot metal oven tray directly into the potato skin; convection circulates hot air around the potato, cooking it from all sides; radiation from the glowing oven elements reaches the potato surface. All three are present. Similarly, a gratin dish cooked in the oven receives convection from the air, conduction through the oven-safe dish, and (if grilled to finish) radiation from above. Top-band answers identify all the methods present and explain why each operates in that cooking context.

Cooking Methods and Nutritive Value

The choice of cooking method has a direct impact on the nutrients remaining in food when it is served. Two key considerations are whether water-soluble vitamins leach out and whether high heat destroys heat-labile nutrients.

Water-soluble vitamins — vitamin C and the B vitamins — dissolve into cooking water and are lost when that water is discarded. Boiling broccoli for ten minutes can destroy 50% or more of its vitamin C. Steaming green vegetables is the spec’s named example of a method that conserves nutritive value: food sits above (not in) the boiling water, so water-soluble vitamins are not leached out. Stir-frying also preserves more vitamin C than boiling because it is fast and uses minimal water. Where boiling is used, using the cooking water in a sauce or soup recovers some of the leached nutrients.

High temperatures modify nutritive value in both directions. Prolonged high-heat roasting of meat destroys B vitamins. However, cooking also increases the availability of some nutrients: cooking tomatoes, for example, increases the bioavailability of lycopene (an antioxidant) because heat breaks down the cell walls. Denaturation of protein through heat improves digestibility — the uncoiled protein is more accessible to digestive enzymes than the tightly folded raw structure.

Improving Palatability Through Cooking

Palatability means how pleasant food is to eat — its flavour, texture, aroma and appearance. Cooking substantially improves palatability through physical denaturation of protein (turning a chewy raw chicken thigh into a tender, juicy one), the Maillard reaction (creating the golden-brown crust and roasted flavour of a loaf of bread or a roasted potato), gelatinisation of starch (thickening a bechamel sauce from a thin liquid to a smooth, coating consistency), and caramelisation of sugars (the amber colour and toffee notes in onions slow-cooked in a pan). These changes make food more attractive, more flavourful and easier to eat, particularly for young children and older adults with reduced appetite.

Positive Uses of Micro-organisms in Food

Not all bacteria are harmful. Some micro-organisms are deliberately used to produce foods that are safer, more flavourful and more varied. The spec identifies three categories where bacteria play a beneficial role:

Dairy products (cheese and yoghurt): Lactic acid bacteria (such as Lactobacillus) convert lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid. In yoghurt-making, this acidification denatures the milk proteins, giving yoghurt its characteristic thick, tangy texture. In cheese-making, bacteria contribute to the development of flavour compounds during ripening, and different bacterial strains produce different cheese styles. The controlled action of bacteria makes the product safer (the acidic pH inhibits pathogens), more digestible and longer-lasting than fresh milk.

Cured meat products (salami and chorizo): Fermentation bacteria are also used in cured sausages. Lactic acid bacteria reduce the pH of the meat mixture, inhibiting the growth of pathogens such as Listeria and Clostridium botulinum. The acid environment also contributes to the firm, tangy character of products like salami and chorizo. The combination of fermentation, salt and drying makes these products shelf-stable without refrigeration.

Fermentation of sugar in drinks: Yeast ferments sugars to produce carbon dioxide (the bubbles in bread and beer) and ethanol. In bread-making, it is the CO2 that matters — the gas pockets created as yeast ferments the sugars in dough cause the loaf to rise. In drinks such as kefir, kombucha and traditional ginger beer, mixed bacterial and yeast cultures ferment sugars to produce a lightly acidic, effervescent drink.

A Sunday roast uses all three heat transfer methods simultaneously. The roasting tin conducts heat up through the base of the joint (conduction). Hot oven air circulates around the joint on all sides (convection). The glowing oven elements emit infrared waves that reach the top surface of the joint and the outer fat layer (radiation), helping to form the golden-brown crust. Meanwhile, the roast potatoes crisp in the goose fat because that fat conducts heat efficiently from the tin into the potato starch layer (conduction), while the circulating hot air browns the exposed surfaces (convection + radiation). Being able to name and explain all three methods in a single dish context is exactly what a top-band answer looks like.

before.description: The ten functional properties of carbohydrates, fats, proteins and fruit and vegetables when cooked.
before.content_html:
Why Ingredients Behave the Way They Do

Every time you make a sauce, bake a cake or fry an egg, you are running a chemistry experiment. The spec identifies ten functional properties — specific chemical or physical changes that occur when ingredients are subjected to heat, liquid, mechanical action or acid. Knowing the correct term, the right ingredient and what happens at a molecular level is the difference between a one-mark recall answer and an eight-mark explanation. This lesson covers all ten, grouped by ingredient type, focusing on familiar dishes and what goes wrong when they fail.

Carbohydrates: Gelatinisation and Dextrinization

Gelatinisation is what happens to starch in a liquid when heated above approximately 60°C. Starch exists as tightly packed granules containing two types of starch molecule: amylose (long straight chains) and amylopectin (branched chains). When the granule is placed in warm liquid and heated, the hydrogen bonds holding the granule together weaken, water molecules force their way in, and the granule swells dramatically. Above about 80°C, the granule bursts, releasing the amylose and amylopectin molecules into the surrounding liquid. These molecules form a tangled network that traps water — the result is the thickening of a sauce, custard, gravy or soup. As the mixture cools, the network becomes more rigid; a cornflour-thickened pudding sets solid in the fridge because the starch molecules form a firm gel on cooling.

A common failure: a lumpy sauce. If starch is added directly to hot liquid, the outer granules gelatinise instantly and form a sticky coating that traps dry starch inside. The fix is to disperse starch in cold liquid or fat first (a slurry or roux), then heat gradually while stirring.

Dextrinization occurs when starch is subjected to dry heat rather than moist heat. The long starch chains are broken by heat into shorter fragments called dextrins. These are sweeter than raw starch, browner in colour and more soluble. The golden-brown crust on toasted bread, the crust on a baked pastry, the coating on roasted potatoes and the surface of a pan of fried rice all involve dextrinization. Unlike gelatinisation (which requires water), dextrinization requires only heat and the absence of water — that is why bread goes golden in a toaster but not in a bowl of water.

Both involve starch and both involve heat, so students conflate them. The key distinction: gelatinisation = starch + water + heat — granules swell and burst, thickening a liquid (a sauce, a custard, a gravy). Dextrinization = starch + dry heat (no water) — starch chains break into dextrins, causing browning and a sweetened, crisped surface (toast crust, pastry crust, roasted potato skin). A bechamel sauce thickening on the hob is gelatinisation. The pastry case turning golden in the oven is dextrinization. They cannot both be the same process because one requires water and the other requires the absence of it.

Fats and Oils: Shortening, Aeration, Plasticity and Emulsification

Shortening occurs when fat coats the flour protein particles, preventing the glutenin and gliadin from combining with water to form gluten. The result is a product with a crumbly, tender, “short” texture. Shortcrust pastry and shortbread both exploit shortening: rubbing cold butter into flour coats the flour in fat before any water is added, limiting gluten formation and giving the characteristic melt-in-the-mouth crumb. The fat is literally “shortening” the gluten network.

Aeration is the incorporation of air bubbles into fat during creaming or whisking. When softened butter and sugar are beaten together (as in the creaming method for a Victoria sandwich), the sugar crystals cut through the fat, creating tiny air pockets that are trapped in the fat. In the oven, these air bubbles expand as the temperature rises, helping the cake to rise and develop a light, open crumb. Without adequate aeration during creaming, the cake will be dense and heavy — a common cause of a sunken, flat sponge.

Plasticity describes the spreadability and workability of solid fats at room temperature. Butter and margarine are plastic: they can be spread, rolled into pastry, shaped and piped because their crystal structure deforms without crumbling. Lard is highly plastic and was traditionally used for pastry, producing particularly short, crumbly results.

Emulsification is the process of combining an oil and a water-based liquid into a stable mixture. Normally, oil and water separate because their molecules are structurally incompatible. An emulsifier has one end that is attracted to water (hydrophilic) and one end attracted to fat (lipophilic). Lecithin in egg yolk is the natural emulsifier in mayonnaise: as the yolk is whisked with vinegar and oil is drizzled in slowly, the lecithin molecules surround tiny oil droplets, keeping them suspended in the vinegar. Remove the egg yolk or add the oil too quickly, and the emulsion splits — the oil and vinegar separate out.

Proteins: Coagulation, Foam Formation, Gluten Formation and Denaturation

Coagulation is the irreversible setting of protein after it has been denatured. When an egg is heated, the protein molecules (albumin in the white, phosvitin and livetin in the yolk) unfold (denature) and then bond together to form a solid network. A perfectly scrambled egg coagulates gently at around 70–80°C, forming soft, creamy curds. Overcooked, it becomes rubbery because excessive heat causes too many cross-links between molecules, squeezing out water. Coagulation also sets the crumb of a cake (egg protein sets around the air bubbles), thickens a custard and firms the interior of a quiche.

Foam formation occurs when egg whites are whisked. Physical action denatures the albumin proteins, causing them to partially unfold and form a film around the air bubbles introduced by whisking. Continuing to whisk builds the foam from soft peaks to stiff peaks. Fat in any form (even a trace of yolk) inhibits foam formation because it coats the protein molecules and prevents them forming a stable film — bowls and whisks must be completely fat-free for meringue.

Gluten formation occurs when wheat flour is mixed with water. Two proteins in the flour — glutenin (strong, elastic) and gliadin (extensible, plastic) — absorb water and link together to form gluten strands. Kneading develops and aligns these strands into a strong, elastic network that can trap carbon dioxide bubbles from yeast fermentation, allowing bread dough to rise and hold its shape during baking. The more a dough is kneaded, the stronger and more elastic the gluten network. Conversely, for shortcrust pastry, gluten development is minimised by using cold fat, cold water and minimal mixing — too much gluten makes pastry tough and difficult to roll.

Denaturation can be caused by heat (cooking an egg), acid (lime juice “cooking” fish in a ceviche — acid denaturation) or physical action (whisking egg whites). Importantly, denaturation is the first step before coagulation — protein first unfolds, then sets. Understanding the distinction matters: a gently warmed egg may partially denature without fully coagulating; an overheated scrambled egg fully coagulates to a rubbery solid.

Key Fact

Ten functional properties to know: Carbohydrates — gelatinisation (sauce thickening), dextrinization (bread crust). Fats/oils — shortening (pastry crumb), aeration (cake rising), plasticity (butter spreading), emulsification (mayonnaise). Protein — coagulation (scrambled eggs setting), foam formation (meringue), gluten formation (bread structure), denaturation (egg white changing on heat).

Key Fact

The emulsifier in egg yolk is lecithin — it has a hydrophilic (water-attracting) end and a lipophilic (fat-attracting) end, which is why mayonnaise holds its oil-in-water structure. Just one drop of yolk in an egg-white foam collapses it, because the fat in the yolk coats the albumin proteins before they can form a stable film around the air bubbles.

Fruit and Vegetables: Enzymic Browning and Oxidisation

Enzymic browning occurs when fruit or vegetables are cut, bruised or damaged. Cells in the produce contain polyphenol oxidase enzymes that are normally kept separate from the phenolic compounds (substrates) also in the tissue. When the cells are disrupted, the enzyme and substrate come into contact, and in the presence of oxygen, a chemical reaction produces brown-coloured melanin pigments. This is why a sliced apple, a cut avocado, a peeled banana or a raw potato turns brown when left exposed to air. To prevent enzymic browning: coat the cut surface with lemon juice or ascorbic acid (vitamin C, which acts as an antioxidant competing for the oxygen), submerge in cold water (limiting oxygen contact), blanch briefly (heat deactivates the enzyme), or refrigerate (cold slows the enzymatic reaction).

Oxidisation is a broader chemical process in which oxygen reacts with food components, causing deterioration. In vegetables, oxidisation of chlorophyll causes colour loss — overcooked broccoli turns dull and khaki as the pigment degrades. Oxidisation of vitamin C during prolonged cooking also reduces nutritional value. In fats, oxidisation causes rancidity — the unpleasant smell and taste of stale cooking oil or old butter. Minimising oxygen exposure through airtight packaging, refrigeration or vacuum packing slows oxidisation in storage.

A sponge cake that sinks in the middle after baking is a classic functional-properties exam scenario. The most likely causes: insufficient aeration during the creaming stage — if the butter was too cold or the creaming time too short, not enough air bubbles were incorporated; too much raising agent — excess carbon dioxide from baking powder creates large bubbles that the protein and starch network cannot support before it has set, so the cake rises then collapses; opening the oven door too early — the cold air rush causes the structure to collapse before the egg protein has fully coagulated; under-baking — starch has not fully gelatinised and egg protein has not fully coagulated, leaving the centre too liquid to hold its shape as the cake cools. The remedy: use butter at room temperature, cream thoroughly until pale and doubled in volume, avoid opening the oven for the first 15 minutes, and check the centre with a skewer before removing.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ten functional properties to know: gelatinisation and dextrinization (carbohydrates); shortening, aeration, plasticity and emulsification (fats/oils); coagulation, foam formation, gluten formation and denaturation (proteins); enzymic browning and oxidisation (fruit/vegetables).
  • Gelatinisation (starch + water + heat → thickened sauce) is distinct from dextrinization (starch + dry heat → golden-brown crust). Coagulation (protein sets irreversibly) follows denaturation (protein unfolds) and cannot be reversed.
  • When desired results are not achieved — a sinking sponge, a lumpy sauce, a split emulsion, enzymic browning on cut apples — there is always a functional-properties explanation. Identifying the property, explaining the failure mechanism and proposing a remedy is exactly what high-tariff exam questions require.
